author: Pranay Mahendrakar
text:
Not every AI user is a Fortune 500 company. Some of the most rewarding work I've done is for small businesses.

A local restaurant wanted to predict daily ingredient needs to reduce food waste. We built a simple time-series model using their POS data and local event calendars. Food waste dropped 35%.

A small e-commerce shop wanted product descriptions in multiple languages. A fine-tuned translation model generates descriptions in 5 languages from a single English input. Their international sales doubled.

A photography studio wanted to automatically sort and tag 50,000 photos. A vision model + simple clustering does it in hours instead of weeks of manual work.

None of these required cutting-edge AI. A gradient boosted tree. A fine-tuned translation model. A pre-trained vision backbone.

The tech was simple. The impact was enormous for businesses operating on thin margins.

What small businesses need from AI isn't a sophisticated architecture. It's a reliable solution that saves them time or money, doesn't require a PhD to maintain, and costs less than hiring another person.

If you can build these kinds of solutions, the market is massive and largely untapped. There are millions of small businesses that could benefit from basic ML but don't know where to start.

Be the engineer who makes AI accessible, not just impressive.

 • How did you evaluate your model’s performance?
 • What did you do to reduce hallucinations?
 • How did you optimize latency and inference costs?
 • How did you measure the business impact of your solution?

These are the discussions that make interviewers believe you can build AI in the real world—not just follow tutorials.

The demand for AI talent is growing rapidly, but companies are becoming far more selective.

They’re looking for engineers who can design, build, evaluate, and deploy reliable AI systems that create business value.

author: Pranav Jadhav
text:
I'm currently pursuing my MCA and actively looking for ML Engineering internships and entry-level roles - remote, hybrid, or relocation all work for me.

Over the past year I've been building full production-style ML systems on my own, not just notebooks - the kind of thing I wanted to be able to point to and say "this actually runs."

The project I'm most proud of: 

a DistilBERT sentiment classifier wrapped in an 8-service Docker Compose stack (Redis, Feast, MLflow, Evidently AI, Nginx, FastAPI, React). It's not just a trained model - it has a feature store for sub-5ms retrieval, canary deployments with automatic rollback, and drift monitoring that flags when the data shifts. Fine-tuned to 92.4% accuracy, and ONNX INT8 quantization cut inference latency by almost half with under 1% accuracy loss.

Alongside that, I've built:

- A RAG-powered document Q&A tool using LangChain + Claude 3.5 Sonnet with hybrid (BM25 + dense) retrieval

- A multi-agent content pipeline (planner → writer → critic) using structured outputs and few-shot prompting

- A LoRA fine-tuning setup for Llama-3-8B on free dual-GPU Kaggle instances, benchmarking throughput and VRAM

I write up what I learn - a few Medium articles and a published model on HuggingFace Hub - because I think the debugging and benchmarking details matter as much as the final result.

I'm looking for a team where I can keep learning by building real things, and where I can contribute from day one.

 If you're hiring ML/MLOps/GenAI interns or entry-level engineers, or know someone who is, I'd love to connect.
